title: ClientStatus: "is it down?" status pages and staff alerts that MSPs give their clients
source: Top 50 research (Nov 2026): reframed from ideas dropped from the Top 25 report, plus new web research
summary: When Microsoft 365, the internet line or an accounting app goes down, every employee at an MSP's client opens a ticket. ClientStatus gives each client a branded status page that pulls Microsoft 365 health, vendor status feeds and the MSP's own alerts, and pushes one message to all staff.
hook: "Outlook went down for two hours and we got 140 tickets that all said the same thing."
story:
**Erik runs a 9-person MSP in Uppsala** with **38 small business clients**. When Microsoft has an Outlook outage or a client's internet provider fails, phones ring nonstop. Every employee at every client asks "is it just me?". His technicians spend the outage answering calls instead of fixing anything.

He tried a generic status page tool, but it is built for software companies announcing their own outages. Erik needs one page **per client**, showing the services *that client* uses (Microsoft 365, their Fortnox or Visma, their line-of-business app, their office internet), filled in automatically, and a button to text and Teams-message all staff: "Known issue, we are on it, next update 14:00." Later the incident list goes into his quarterly client review.
whyNow: Small businesses depend on more cloud services than ever, and MSPs are under pressure to show value and cut ticket volume. Microsoft exposes service health through its Graph API, and many vendors publish status feeds, so an automatic per-client page is now easy to build.
evidence: Atlassian Statuspage has no free tier and starts at about $29/month; Instatus has a free plan and Pro at $20/month; Better Stack white-label pages cost $208–250/month (vendor-authored comparisons) [openstatus / WizStatus / Better Stack]
StatusGator, which aggregates vendor status pages, has a free plan with 3 monitors and paid tiers reported at $79, $149 and $299 per month (competitor comparison) [Pulsetic]
MSPs report manual, fragmented client reporting [Sophos via Top 25 notes]
Status pages and dunning were judged "red oceans" for newcomers unless aimed at a sharp sub-niche such as white-label pages for MSPs [Top 25 research notes]

whyReal.title: Outages create ticket storms
whyReal.text: One cloud outage turns into dozens of identical calls per client. Every avoided call saves technician time.

whyReal.title: Existing tools face the wrong way
whyReal.text: Status page tools are built for software vendors talking to their users. MSPs need one page per client, filled from other vendors' status.

whyReal.title: Visible value for the MSP
whyReal.text: A branded page and proactive messages make the MSP look professional and feed the quarterly review.

whyReal.title: Cheap and quick to build
whyReal.text: Mostly polling public feeds and Microsoft's service-health API; a working MVP in about 5 weeks.

whoPays.label: Buyer
whoPays.text: The MSP owner or service desk manager.

whoPays.label: Start market
whoPays.text: Global in English: UK, Nordics, Australia and US MSP communities; same buyer as InsureReady and QBR Autopilot.

solution.title: Add a client
solution.text: pick the services that client uses from a list (Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, Fortnox, Xero, Zoom, their ISP) and connect their Microsoft tenant read-only.

solution.title: Automatic page
solution.text: a branded page per client shows green/yellow/red for each service, filled from vendor status feeds and Microsoft service health.

solution.title: MSP's own alerts
solution.text: the MSP's monitoring tool can post incidents ("office internet down") through a webhook or email.

solution.title: One-click broadcast
solution.text: send a message to all client staff by email, SMS or Teams, with scheduled updates.

solution.title: Incident history
solution.text: a log per client, exported into quarterly reviews.

must: Service catalogue with vendor status feeds
Email broadcast to client staff lists
later: Ticket deflection banner in the client portal

timeline.what: Jonatan interviews 15 MSPs about the last big outage and ticket counts. Build a static demo page for one MSP.
Service catalogue, feed pollers, per-client pages, branding.
Microsoft service health, broadcasts, incident log, Stripe.
5 pilot MSPs; measure tickets during the next outage.

competitors.name: Atlassian Statuspage, Instatus, Better Stack
competitors.gap: One page about your own service; white-label is expensive or manual

competitors.name: StatusGator
competitors.what: Aggregates vendor status pages, has a public page
competitors.gap: Strongest rival; built for IT teams, not one branded page and broadcast list per MSP client

competitors.name: PSA/RMM tools
competitors.gap: Internal; clients do not see a simple public status

competitors.name: Us
competitors.what: Per-client branded status pages filled from vendor feeds, plus staff broadcasts
competitors.gap: Built for MSPs, priced per MSP not per page

risks.answer: Validate with ticket counts during real outages; sell only if MSPs can show saved hours.
Stay focused on per-client branding, broadcasts and QBR export; bundle with other MSP modules.
Treat it as a cheap entry product into the MSP bundle (InsureReady, QBR Autopilot), not a standalone big business.

questions: During the last Microsoft or internet outage, how many tickets and calls did you get?
How do you tell clients' staff about known issues today?
Do you use a status page now? Why or why not?
Which services do most of your clients depend on?
Would $49–99 a month for branded client status pages be worth it?

numbers.competition: Many status tools; MSP angle thin
